content:
Let the 400 sites be vertices of a graph, with an edge between two sites exactly when their squared distance is  
\[
(x_2-x_1)^2+(y_2-y_1)^2=5,
\]
i.e. a knight’s move. Amy’s red stones must form an independent set in this graph.

**Lower bound.** Amy can always play on sites with \(x+y\) even. There are \(200\) such sites, and no two of them are a knight’s move apart. Before Amy’s \(100\)th move, Ben has placed at most \(99\) blue stones, so even if all of them are on even sites, at most \(99+99=198\) of the \(200\) even sites are occupied. Hence Amy can place a \(100\)th red stone. Thus
\[
K\ge 100.
\]

**Upper bound.** Partition the \(20\times 20\) board into \(25\) blocks of size \(4\times 4\). In each \(4\times 4\) block, with coordinates \((0,0)\) to \((3,3)\), partition the \(16\) sites into the following four 4-cycles of knight moves:
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(0,1),(1,3),(3,2),(2,0);\\
&(0,0),(1,2),(3,3),(2,1);\\
&(0,2),(1,0),(3,1),(2,3);\\
&(0,3),(1,1),(3,0),(2,2).
\end{aligned}
\]
This gives \(25\cdot 4=100\) disjoint 4-cycles.

Ben’s strategy: whenever Amy plays in one of these 4-cycles, Ben plays the opposite vertex of that same 4-cycle. Then the other two vertices of the cycle are each a knight’s move from Amy’s red stone, so Amy can never use them. Thus each 4-cycle contains at most one red stone. Since there are \(100\) cycles,
\[
K\le 100.
\]

Therefore,
\[
\boxed{100}.
\]
